pos: n. (the quality of being salt; savour, pungency)
etymology: From salt, Old English sealt, with the suffix -ness. The Greek is halas with the verb analos ginomai, to become saltless. Mark's Gospel uses the noun where Matthew uses savour.
biblical_def: Our Lord ends a severe passage on self-denial with a word about salt: “Salt is good: but if the salt have lost his saltness, wherewith will ye season it? Have salt in yourselves, and have peace one with another” (Mark 9:50). Saltness is the property that makes salt salt — its savour, its pungency, its power to season and preserve. The warning turns on the one thing salt cannot recover. Many spoiled things can be restored; a lost saltness cannot be re-salted, because salt is the only thing that salts. Matthew records the same saying with the same force: “Ye are the salt of the earth: but if the salt have lost his savour, wherewith shall it be salted? it is thenceforth good for nothing” (Matthew 5:13). The two halves of Mark's verse belong together. Have salt in yourselves is distinctness, the preserving sharpness of a holy people; have peace one with another is the use to which that sharpness is put, since the disciples had just been disputing who was greatest. Paul draws the same line through Christian speech: “Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt” (Colossians 4:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): SALTNESS, the quality of being impregnated with salt; taste of salt.
webster_full: SALTNESS, n. The quality of being impregnated with salt; the taste of salt.
SALT, n. Common salt, used for seasoning and preserving.
SALT, a. Having the taste of salt; pungent; sharp.

corruption_summary: Saltiness is taken as either abrasiveness or likeness to the world, so that the church is urged to be either harsher or blander than Christ made her.
corruption_paragraphs: One party reads this text as a licence for pugnacity. Salt stings, therefore the Christian should sting, and online combativeness is baptised as savour. Mark forecloses it in the same breath: have salt in yourselves, and have peace one with another. The disciples who first heard it had been arguing about rank, and the command to be salty was a rebuke of that dispute, not its fuel.

The other party reads the loss of saltness as a problem of accessibility, and prescribes a church indistinguishable in doctrine, worship and morals from the world it addresses. That is the very thing Christ calls good for nothing. Salt works by being different from the meat; the moment it is not, it preserves nothing and is trodden under foot. The church's usefulness and her distinctness are the same thing, and neither harshness nor blandness is savour.

pos: n. (scarcity; want, the condition of having too little)
etymology: From scarce, Old French escars, sparing or niggardly, from Late Latin excarpsus, plucked out, with the suffix -ness. The Hebrew miskenuth means poverty or want.
biblical_def: Describing the land Israel was about to enter, Moses stacks up abundance: “A land wherein thou shalt eat bread without scarceness, thou shalt not lack any thing in it; a land whose stones are iron, and out of whose hills thou mayest dig brass” (Deuteronomy 8:9). Scarceness is scarcity, and the promise is bread without it. But the whole chapter is a warning wrapped around that promise, and the danger named is not famine but fullness. Two verses later: “When thou hast eaten and art full, then thou shalt bless the LORD thy God for the good land which he hath given thee” (Deuteronomy 8:10) — and then the long caution that the heart be not lifted up to say, my power and the might of mine hand hath gotten me this wealth. Moses supplies the correction: “But thou shalt remember the LORD thy God: for it is he that giveth thee power to get wealth, that he may establish his covenant which he sware unto thy fathers” (Deuteronomy 8:18). The absence of scarceness is therefore the sharpest test in the chapter. Forty years of manna had taught dependence; a land of iron and brass would test whether the lesson held.

corruption_summary: Deuteronomy 8:18 is lifted out of its warning and preached as a promise of personal wealth, when in its place it is the antidote to the pride that wealth breeds.
corruption_paragraphs: “It is he that giveth thee power to get wealth” is among the most frequently abused verses in prosperity preaching, printed on conference banners and quoted as a guarantee of increase. The abuse works by amputation. Moses is not promising riches; he is warning a nation about to become rich, and the clause is the reason they must remember the LORD rather than credit their own hand.

Read whole, the chapter cuts both ways. It forbids the asceticism that treats plenty as inherently corrupt, for the land of iron and brass is God's good gift and Israel is commanded to eat and be full and bless Him. And it forbids the self-congratulation that reads prosperity as proof of favour earned, for the stated end of the wealth is that God may establish His covenant. Bread without scarceness is a mercy and a test in the same loaf.

etymology: From few, Old English feawe, with the suffix -ness. The Hebrew phrase is mispar shanim, the number of years, rendered by the single English noun.
biblical_def: The law of the jubilee includes a rule of just pricing: “According to the multitude of years thou shalt increase the price thereof, and according to the fewness of years thou shalt diminish the price of it: for according to the number of the years of the fruits doth he sell unto thee” (Leviticus 25:16). Fewness is smallness of number, here of the years remaining before the jubilee. Since the land reverted to its family in the fiftieth year, nobody ever bought land in Israel; a man bought a number of harvests, and the price had to reflect exactly how many. Many years, higher price; few years, lower. The rule is simple, and it is the law of honest dealing applied to the one asset that could not be permanently alienated: “And ye shall hallow the fiftieth year, and proclaim liberty throughout all the land unto all the inhabitants thereof: it shall be a jubile unto you” (Leviticus 25:10). God gives the reason He legislates the price at all: “Ye shall not therefore oppress one another; but thou shalt fear thy God: for I am the LORD your God” (Leviticus 25:17). Fear of God is the ground of a fair price, and the land was never anyone's to keep.

webster_full: FEWNESS, n. Smallness of number; paucity.

corruption_summary: The jubilee is enlisted as a mandate for modern debt-cancellation programmes, and its covenantal basis in a land God calls His own is dropped.
corruption_paragraphs: Liberation theology and a great deal of activist preaching treat Leviticus 25 as a blueprint for contemporary economic policy: cancel the debts, redistribute the land, proclaim a jubilee. The text is then detached from its ground, which is that this particular land was given to these particular families by covenant, and that the LORD says plainly, the land is mine. No modern state stands in Israel's place, and no programme inherits her statute.

Losing the covenantal ground also loses the doctrine the chapter actually teaches, which is weightier than policy. God legislates the price of a field so that His people will not oppress one another, and gives as the reason, thou shalt fear thy God. The jubilee's fulfilment is announced by Christ in the synagogue at Nazareth: the acceptable year of the LORD, liberty to the captives. Honest pricing remains binding on every believer; the jubilee itself has met its substance.

pos: n. (the state of being old; the old condition or manner)
etymology: From old, Old English eald, with the suffix -ness. The Greek is palaiotes, antiquatedness, from palaios, old, and it carries the sense of what is worn out and superseded.
biblical_def: Paul sets two services against each other in a single clause: “But now we are delivered from the law, that being dead wherein we were held; that we should serve in newness of spirit, and not in the oldness of the letter” (Romans 7:6). The Greek palaiotes is not merely age but obsolescence: a worn-out mode of service. The oldness of the letter is the attempt to be righteous by the written code as a covenant of works, an attempt the law itself exposes as impossible. What the believer is delivered from is not God's moral law as a rule of life, for Paul in the next verses calls the law holy, just and good, and says he delights in it after the inward man. What he is delivered from is the law as a way of justification, and from the service rendered under it. The deliverance comes by union: “ye also are become dead to the law by the body of Christ; that ye should be married to another, even to him who is raised from the dead” (Romans 7:4). And the contrast is the apostolic ministry's own: “the letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life” (2 Corinthians 3:6).

corruption_summary: Romans 7:6 is read as abolishing God's moral law for the Christian, so that antinomianism borrows Paul's words to say what Paul immediately denies.
corruption_paragraphs: Antinomianism in all its forms, from the radical reformers to modern grace movements that forbid preaching the commandments to believers, leans on this verse. Delivered from the law, serving not in the oldness of the letter: the words seem to retire the Decalogue. Paul's own next sentence refuses it — is the law sin? God forbid — and he goes on to call the commandment holy, just and good, and to delight in the law of God after the inward man.

The confessional distinction is the one Paul makes. The law as a covenant of works, offering life on condition of perfect obedience, is dead to the believer because Christ fulfilled it and bore its curse; the law as a rule of life remains, written now on the heart by the Spirit. That is the newness of spirit: the same commandments, obeyed from a new nature, by a new power, with a new motive. Legalism and antinomianism are both the oldness of the letter wearing different clothes.

etymology: From large, Latin largus, abundant, plentiful, with the suffix -ness. The Hebrew rochab leb is breadth of heart, the same word for breadth used of a measured space.
biblical_def: The gift Solomon received is described in three terms: “And God gave Solomon wisdom and understanding exceeding much, and largeness of heart, even as the sand that is on the sea shore” (1 Kings 4:29). Largeness of heart is breadth of heart, a capacity of mind and affection wide enough to take in the whole range of things God had made; the next verses describe him speaking of trees, beasts, fowl, creeping things and fishes, and uttering three thousand proverbs. The measure given is the sand on the sea shore, the same figure used of Abraham's seed. And the gift was asked for, not assumed: “Give therefore thy servant an understanding heart to judge thy people, that I may discern between good and bad” (1 Kings 3:9). Solomon asked for discernment to govern and received largeness besides. James holds the door open on the same terms: “If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God, that giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not” (James 1:5). The sorrow of Solomon's story is that largeness of heart is not the same as a guarded heart; the wisest man turned aside, and Scripture records it plainly.

corruption_summary: Largeness of heart is confused with breadth of conviction, so that doctrinal indifference calls itself magnanimity and a mind that holds nothing firmly is praised as wide.
corruption_paragraphs: A certain kind of ecumenism has borrowed this phrase. Largeness of heart becomes the virtue of holding no position too firmly, of finding something commendable in every framework, of refusing to call error by its name. The man of large heart, on that account, is the man of soft edges. Scripture gives the phrase to a king who wrote Proverbs, a book that divides the world sharply into wisdom and folly and has nothing good to say of the scorner.

Largeness in 1 Kings 4 is capacity, not indifference: a heart wide enough for trees and beasts and fishes and three thousand proverbs, held by a man who had asked God for power to discern between good and bad. Nor does it guarantee perseverance; the same king's heart was turned away by his wives, and the Spirit records it for our warning. Ask for largeness, and guard the heart that receives it.

pos: n. (skill, dexterity; practised competence in a work)
etymology: From skilful, from skill, Old Norse skil, discernment or distinction, with -ful and -ness. The Hebrew tebunah means understanding or discernment, here applied to the hands.
biblical_def: The seventy-eighth Psalm ends its long rehearsal of Israel's history with God's choice of David: “So he fed them according to the integrity of his heart; and guided them by the skilfulness of his hands” (Psalm 78:72). Two things are named and both are necessary. Integrity of heart is character; skilfulness of hands is competence. The Hebrew behind skilfulness is a word for understanding, so this is not raw dexterity but practised discernment expressing itself in work. And the metaphor is deliberately pastoral, for David had been taken from the sheepfolds: “From following the ewes great with young he brought him to feed Jacob his people, and Israel his inheritance” (Psalm 78:71). The man who had learned to handle ewes heavy with young was given a nation to handle. The pairing is the standing biblical pattern for leadership. An elder must be blameless and also apt to teach; a craftsman must be godly and also able; a father must be faithful and also competent. Integrity without skill fumbles the flock; skill without integrity fleeces it. God gave Israel a shepherd who had both.

corruption_summary: Leadership is reduced to either sincerity without competence or competence without character, when Scripture requires both of the same man.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the pairing in the verse: integrity of heart and skilfulness of hands, held together in one shepherd.

Churches fail on both sides. One sort appoints the sincere and untrained and then endures years of avoidable damage, calling the damage spiritual. Another sort recruits for competence, charisma and executive gift, overlooks the walk, and discovers the cost later. The pastoral epistles pair the two as Psalm 78 does: blameless, and apt to teach. The man who tended ewes heavy with young was being trained in both at once, and God gave him to Israel as a shepherd of hands as well as heart.

pos: n. pl. (bankers; money-changers who received deposits and paid interest)
etymology: From exchange, Old French eschangier, from Late Latin excambiare, to barter. The Greek trapezites is literally a table-man, from trapeza, a table, the banker's counter; hence a banker.
biblical_def: In the parable of the talents the lord answers the servant who buried his trust: “Thou oughtest therefore to have put my money to the exchangers, and then at my coming I should have received mine own with usury” (Matthew 25:27). The exchangers are bankers, the Greek trapezitai, men who sat at tables receiving deposits and paying a return. The force of the rebuke lies in how little was required. The servant need not have traded, risked or innovated; he could have handed the money to a banker and let it earn. He did not even do that. His sin was not failure in business but refusal of stewardship, defended by a slander against his master's character: I knew that thou art an hard man. The parable's two outcomes are stated plainly. To the faithful: “Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things” (Matthew 25:21). To the other: “And cast ye the unprofitable servant into outer darkness: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matthew 25:30). Nothing entrusted by Christ may be buried.

corruption_summary: The parable is turned into a lesson about financial investment or natural talent, and its actual subject — accountability to Christ at His coming, with eternal consequence — is set aside.
corruption_paragraphs: Two misreadings are common. The prosperity reading makes the parable a divine endorsement of investment returns, as though Christ were teaching portfolio management; the motivational reading makes talents mean natural abilities and the lesson a call to self-actualisation. The English word has drifted far enough that the second is almost unavoidable in casual use: a talent in Matthew 25 is a weight of silver, not a knack.

The parable's subject is the return of the Lord and the reckoning He will hold. The servants are stewards of what is not theirs; the issue is faithfulness; and the verdict for the man who buried his trust is outer darkness, weeping and gnashing of teeth. Christ's own words forbid both annihilationism and universalism here. Every believer holds something in trust — the gospel, a household, an office, a purse, a day — and the exchangers stand in the text to show how slight an excuse unfaithfulness really has.

pos: v. (past participle; priced, valued, appraised at a sum)
etymology: From Old French prisier, to value, from Latin pretium, price. Prise in older English means to set a price on, to appraise; prize in the sense of esteeming highly is the same root. The Hebrew yaqar means to be valued or esteemed.
biblical_def: The shepherd-prophet of Zechariah 11, rejected by the flock he fed, asks for his wages and is paid thirty pieces of silver. God's answer is bitter irony: “And the LORD said unto me, Cast it unto the potter: a goodly price that I was prised at of them. And I took the thirty pieces of silver, and cast them to the potter in the house of the LORD” (Zechariah 11:13). To be prised is to be priced, appraised at a sum. The sum was the compensation for a dead slave under the law of Exodus 21, and the speaker is the LORD Himself in the person of His shepherd: this is what Israel reckoned Him worth. The whole transaction had been set up two verses earlier: “So they weighed for my price thirty pieces of silver” (Zechariah 11:12). Five centuries later Matthew records the fulfilment to the coin, the man, the sum and the destination: “And they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of him that was valued, whom they of the children of Israel did value” (Matthew 27:9). Judas, the priests, the potter's field: every detail of the prophecy came in.

corruption_summary: The thirty pieces are explained as a detail Matthew read backwards into Zechariah, denying genuine predictive prophecy and the sovereignty that governed the betrayal.
corruption_paragraphs: The standard critical account runs thus: the Gospel writers searched the prophets for texts that could be bent to fit events, and Matthew's citation here — which names Jeremy where the words stand in Zechariah — proves the method was careless. On that reading there is no prophecy, only retrofitting. The dictionary rejects the premise. Scripture declares the end from the beginning, and Matthew's composite citation follows a recognised Jewish convention of naming the greater prophet in whose roll the collection stood, with Jeremiah's own potter and field in view.

What the critical reading destroys is the doctrine of the two causes in the betrayal. Judas sold freely and is guilty; the price, the field and the potter were determined before Judas was born. Peter preaches both at Pentecost: delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God, and by wicked hands crucified and slain. The thirty pieces of silver are the hinge of that doctrine, and the prophecy insists upon it with heavy irony — a goodly price.

pos: n. (one who raises; in the phrase a raiser of taxes, an exactor of tribute)
etymology: Agent noun from raise, Old Norse reisa, to cause to rise. The Hebrew phrase in Daniel 11:20 pairs a participle of abar, to cause to pass over, with noges, an exactor; hence one who makes tribute pass to the treasury.
biblical_def: In the long prophecy of Daniel 11 one king is identified by his revenue policy: “Then shall stand up in his estate a raiser of taxes in the glory of the kingdom: but within few days he shall be destroyed, neither in anger, nor in battle” (Daniel 11:20). A raiser of taxes is an exactor of tribute, and the prophecy is uncannily specific: this king is remembered for nothing but his exactions, he reigns briefly, and he dies neither by assassination in anger nor by defeat in battle. The history answered to it in Seleucus IV Philopator, whose minister was sent to plunder the temple treasury and who died by treachery after a short reign. The next verse introduces the vile person who obtains the kingdom by flatteries (Daniel 11:21). Scripture does not condemn taxation as such — “Render therefore to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due; custom to whom custom” (Romans 13:7) — and Christ paid tribute and told Israel to render unto Caesar. What Daniel marks is a ruler whose whole character is exaction: a throne used as a tax-farm, and a reign God cut short.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): RAISER, one who raises; one that builds, erects, or exalts; one who levies or exacts.
webster_full: RAISER, n. One who raises; one who builds.
He that exalts or elevates; one that levies or collects.
RAISE, v.t. To lift; to exalt; to levy, as to raise a tax or an army.
Hebrew noges, an exactor or taskmaster.
Daniel 11:20 foretells a raiser of taxes who is destroyed within few days.
scriptures: Then shall stand up in his estate a raiser of taxes in the glory of the kingdom: but within few days he shall be destroyed, neither in anger, nor in battle.
And in his estate shall stand up a vile person, to whom they shall not give the honour of the kingdom: but he shall come in peaceably, and obtain the kingdom by flatteries.
Rom 13:7
Render therefore to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due; custom to whom custom; fear to whom fear; honour to whom honour.
corruption_summary: Daniel 11 is dated after the events it foretells in order to deny predictive prophecy, and the result is a Bible that cannot announce the end from the beginning.
corruption_paragraphs: The detail of Daniel 11 is so exact that critical scholarship almost universally dates the book to the second century before Christ, after the events described, treating it as history written as prophecy. The dictionary holds the sixth-century Daniel of the text itself, as our Lord did when He spoke of the abomination of desolation spoken of by Daniel the prophet. The late dating is not a conclusion drawn from evidence but a requirement of a method that has excluded prediction in advance.

What is at stake is larger than one book. The God of Scripture declares the end from the beginning, and that claim is the ground of every promise a believer rests on. A Daniel written after the fact proves nothing about the Seleucids and promises nothing about the kingdom that shall never be destroyed. Meanwhile the verse's plain political lesson stands: tribute is lawfully owed, and a ruler who is nothing but an exactor has a short reign recorded against him.
roots_summary: Agent noun from raise; Hebrew noges, an exactor; Daniel 11:20 foretells a raiser of taxes destroyed within few days.
roots_lines: Old Norse reisa, to cause to rise, gives raise and raiser.
Hebrew noges, an exactor or taskmaster.
Daniel 11:20 is the only occurrence of raiser in the Authorized Version.
The king dies neither in anger nor in battle, a doubly precise detail.
Romans 13:7 affirms that tribute is lawfully owed.
usage: a raiser of taxes in the glory of the kingdom
names a ruler remembered for nothing but exaction
set in a prophecy of exact predictive detail

pos: v. (to furnish with a dower; to settle a bride-price or portion upon a woman)
etymology: From Old French endouer, from Latin in and dotare, to endow, from dos, a dowry. To endow a woman is to settle a portion on her. The Hebrew mahar means to pay the bride-price.
biblical_def: The civil law of Exodus protects a seduced woman by binding the man to her: “And if a man entice a maid that is not betrothed, and lie with her, he shall surely endow her to be his wife” (Exodus 22:16). To endow is to pay the mohar, the bride-price settled on a woman and her house at marriage. The law gives the man no option of walking away: having taken what belonged to her future husband, he becomes that husband and pays in full. The father retains a protection for his daughter: “If her father utterly refuse to give her unto him, he shall pay money according to the dowry of virgins” (Exodus 22:17) — the price is owed whether or not the marriage proceeds. Deuteronomy sets the sum and closes the escape: “Then the man that lay with her shall give unto the damsel's father fifty shekels of silver, and she shall be his wife; because he hath humbled her, he may not put her away all his days” (Deuteronomy 22:29). Far from treating women as property, these statutes make seduction expensive and permanent for the man and secure for the woman, in an ancient world where she would otherwise have been ruined.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): ENDOW, to furnish with a portion of estate; to settle a dower on a woman; to enrich with any gift.
webster_full: ENDOW, v.t. To furnish with a portion of estate or wealth, as a woman at marriage.
To settle a dower on; as, he endowed his wife.
To enrich or furnish with any gift, quality or faculty.
From Latin dos, a dowry, through Old French endouer.
Exodus 22:16 says he shall surely endow her to be his wife.
scriptures: And if a man entice a maid that is not betrothed, and lie with her, he shall surely endow her to be his wife.
If her father utterly refuse to give her unto him, he shall pay money according to the dowry of virgins.
Then the man that lay with her shall give unto the damsel's father fifty shekels of silver, and she shall be his wife; because he hath humbled her, he may not put her away all his days.
corruption_summary: The bride-price statutes are cited as proof that Scripture treats women as goods to be bought, when their plain effect is to bind the man and shield the woman.
corruption_paragraphs: These verses are standard exhibits in the progressive case against biblical sexual ethics, offered as evidence of a patriarchy that sold daughters and forced victims to marry their seducers. The dictionary rejects that reading of the text and the explanatory category it comes wrapped in. Scripture's account of the world is sin, covenant and curse, not autonomous power structures; and the law in question is one of the most protective in the ancient Near East.

Read the statute's actual effects. The man loses every option: he pays the full bride-price whether he marries her or not, he may never divorce her, and the father may veto the match while still collecting the money. The woman, who in that world would have been left unmarriageable and destitute, is made secure for life at his expense. The separate law of Deuteronomy 22:25-27 deals with force and puts the man to death. The intent throughout is to make a man's lust cost him everything and to leave the woman whole.
roots_summary: Latin dos, a dowry; Hebrew mahar, to pay the bride-price; Exodus 22:16 binds the seducer to endow the woman as his wife.
roots_lines: Latin dos, a dowry, with in and dotare: to settle a portion upon.
Hebrew mahar, to pay the mohar or bride-price.
Exodus 22:16 is the only occurrence of endow in the Authorized Version.
The price is owed even if the father refuses the marriage (Exodus 22:17).
Deuteronomy 22:29 fixes fifty shekels and forbids divorce for life.
